We train decoder-only transformers (up to 700M parameters) on these datasets and show that CoT accelerates the accuracy transition to higher values across model sizes. In particular, we find that model depth is crucial for leveraging CoT with limited in-context examples, while more examples help shallow models match deeper model performance. Additionally, limiting the diversity of token processing functions throughout training improves causal structure learning via ICL. We also interpret these transitions by analyzing transformer embeddings and attention maps. Overall, CoT-ICL Lab serves as a simple yet powerful testbed for theoretical and empirical insights into ICL and CoT in language models.

papers.title: Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models exhibit human-like intuitive reasoning errors, and how do more advanced models avoid these errors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs exhibit human-like intuitive errors (System 1), but more advanced models (ChatGPT, GPT-4) avoid these errors through chain-of-thought reasoning and well-developed intuition, performing hyperrationally.
papers.conclusion: Psychological methods can reveal emergent traits in LLMs; advanced LLMs show remarkable reasoning abilities and can avoid intuitive errors, resembling both System 1 and System 2 processes.
papers.key_findings:
Early/smaller LLMs (up to GPT-3-curie) often give atypical responses, indicating poor task comprehension.
Larger pre-ChatGPT models (GPT-3-davinci family) show a high tendency to give intuitive but incorrect responses, similar to human System 1 errors.
ChatGPT models (especially GPT-4) show a high fraction of correct responses, often using chain-of-thought reasoning.
Instructing GPT-3-davinci-003 to use chain-of-thought reasoning reduces intuitive errors and increases correct responses.
Providing training examples (few-shot) improves GPT-3-davinci-003's performance on both CRT and semantic illusions.
papers.limitation:
The study only tested one family of LLMs (the GPT family).
The tasks used are limited in scope (CRT and semantic illusions).
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LLMs is not truly deliberate System 2 reasoning but resembles it.
papers.abstract: We design a battery of semantic illusions and cognitive reflection tests, aimed to elicit intuitive yet erroneous responses. We administer these tasks, traditionally used to study reasoning and decision-making in humans, to OpenAI's generative pre-trained transformer model family. The results show that as the models expand in size and linguistic proficiency they increasingly display human-like intuitive system 1 thinking and associated cognitive errors. This pattern shifts notably with the introduction of ChatGPT models, which tend to respond correctly, avoiding the traps embedded in the tasks. Both ChatGPT-3.5 and 4 utilize the input-output context window to engage in chain-of-thought reasoning, reminiscent of how people use notepads to support their system 2 thinking. Yet, they remain accurate even when prevented from engaging in chain-of-thought reasoning, indicating that their system-1-like next-word generation processes are more accurate than those of older models. Our findings highlight the value of applying psychological methodologies to study large language models, as this can uncover previously undetected emergent characteristics.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning Enhances Existing Mechanisms: A Case Study on Entity Tracking
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the internal mechanisms for entity tracking in language models? Specifically, does fine-tuning change the circuit for entity tracking, how does the circuit work, and what specific sub-mechanism is improved?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning enhances existing mechanisms rather than fundamentally altering them; the same entity tracking circuit is present and functional in both base and fine-tuned models, with performance gains due to improved handling of positional information.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning enhances existing mechanisms rather than fundamentally altering them.
papers.key_findings:
The same entity tracking circuit is present in both base and fine-tuned models.
The circuit functionality remains the same: entity tracking is performed by tracking the position of the correct entity.
Performance improvement in fine-tuned models is primarily due to improved handling of augmented positional information.
The circuit in fine-tuned models is larger (superset of the base circuit) but the core mechanism is the same.
Cross-model activation patching (CMAP) can localize the improved sub-mechanism.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to a single task (entity tracking) and a few models (Llama-7B and its fine-tuned variants).
future_direction: Extend the study to more tasks and models.
Investigate whether the enhancement of existing mechanisms is a general principle.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning on generalized tasks such as instruction following, code generation, and mathematics has been shown to enhance language models' performance on a range of tasks. Nevertheless, explanations of how such fine-tuning influences the internal computations in these models remain elusive. We study how fine-tuning affects the internal mechanisms implemented in language models. As a case study, we explore the property of entity tracking, a crucial facet of language comprehension, where models fine-tuned on mathematics have substantial performance gains. We identify the mechanism that enables entity tracking and show that (i) in both the original model and its fine-tuned versions primarily the same circuit implements entity tracking. In fact, the entity tracking circuit of the original model on the fine-tuned versions performs better than the full original model. (ii) The circuits of all the models implement roughly the same functionality: Entity tracking is performed by tracking the position of the correct entity in both the original model and its fine-tuned versions. (iii) Performance boost in the fine-tuned models is primarily attributed to its improved ability to handle the augmented positional information. To uncover these findings, we employ: Patch Patching, DCM, which automatically detects model components responsible for specific semantics, and CMAP, a new approach for patching activations across models to reveal improved mechanisms. Our findings suggest that fine-tuning enhances, rather than fundamentally alters, the mechanistic operation of the model.

papers.title: Don't Take Things Out of Context: Attention Intervention for Enhancing Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the mechanism by which isolated tokens in few-shot Chain-of-Thought demonstrations disrupt reasoning in LLMs, and how can we intervene to suppress this effect?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Few-shot Attention Intervention (FAI), a method that dynamically analyzes attention patterns to identify and suppress the distracting effect of isolated tokens in CoT demonstrations, thereby enhancing reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: FAI effectively recalibrates attention allocation to prevent LLMs from fixating on isolated tokens, enhancing reasoning performance across benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
Isolated tokens in CoT demonstrations can disrupt reasoning by causing the model to take information out of context.
Tokens with specific attention characteristics (high self-attention, direct influence on output) are responsible for this distracting effect.
FAI effectively identifies such tokens and improves performance across multiple reasoning benchmarks.
FAI improves accuracy on AQuA by 5.91% and on other datasets.
The distracting effect is estimated to cause about 60% of errors in certain cases.
papers.limitation: Experiments are confined to LLMs with parameter scale between 7 billion and 13 billion due to hardware constraints.
future_direction: Investigating larger models to gain further insights.
papers.abstract: Few-shot Chain-of-Thought (CoT) significantly enhances the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), functioning as a whole to guide these models in generating reasoning steps toward final answers. However, we observe that isolated segments, words, or tokens within CoT demonstrations can unexpectedly disrupt the generation process of LLMs. The model may overly concentrate on certain local information present in the demonstration, introducing irrelevant noise into the reasoning process and potentially leading to incorrect answers. In this paper, we investigate the underlying mechanism of CoT through dynamically tracing and manipulating the inner workings of LLMs at each output step, which demonstrates that tokens exhibiting specific attention characteristics are more likely to induce the model to take things out of context; these tokens directly attend to the hidden states tied with prediction, without substantial integration of non-local information. Building upon these insights, we propose a Few-shot Attention Intervention method (FAI) that dynamically analyzes the attention patterns of demonstrations to accurately identify these tokens and subsequently make targeted adjustments to the attention weights to effectively suppress their distracting effect on LLMs. Comprehensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over baseline methods, with a remarkable 5.91% improvement on the AQuA dataset, further highlighting the effectiveness of FAI.

papers.title: Mechanistic Indicators of Understanding in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) possess genuine understanding, and if so, what forms does it take? The paper investigates this by synthesizing findings from mechanistic interpretability within a philosophical framework.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a tiered framework (conceptual, state-of-the-world, principled understanding) for assessing understanding in LLMs and synthesizes mechanistic interpretability evidence to argue that LLMs can develop internal organizations that underwrite understanding-like unification, though these mechanisms diverge from human cognition.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability reveals internal organizations in LLMs that can underwrite understanding-like unification across conceptual, factual, and principled tiers, but these mechanisms diverge from human cognition in their parallel exploitation of heterogeneous, task-specific pathways.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs develop internal 'features' (e.g., a 'Golden Gate Bridge' feature in Claude 3 Sonnet) that act as conceptual unifiers, connecting diverse manifestations of entities or properties.
The linear representation hypothesis is supported, with features encoded as directions in latent space, and superposition allows for efficient representation of many features.
Models like Othello-GPT develop internal 'world models' (e.g., of the board state) that are causally involved in task performance, as shown via probing and intervention techniques.
The phenomenon of 'grokking' demonstrates a shift from memorization to discovering compact, generalizable circuits (e.g., for modular arithmetic), indicative of principled understanding.
Higher-tier understanding mechanisms coexist with lower-tier heuristics (e.g., memorization, n-gram statistics) within LLMs, impacting their epistemic trustworthiness.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often portrayed as merely imitating linguistic patterns without genuine understanding. We argue that recent findings in mechanistic interpretability (MI), the emerging field probing the inner workings of LLMs, render this picture increasingly untenable--but only once those findings are integrated within a theoretical account of understanding. We propose a tiered framework for thinking about understanding in LLMs and use it to synthesize the most relevant findings to date. The framework distinguishes three hierarchical varieties of understanding, each tied to a corresponding level of computational organization: conceptual understanding emerges when a model forms "features" as directions in latent space, learning connections between diverse manifestations of a single entity or property; state-of-the-world understanding emerges when a model learns contingent factual connections between features and dynamically tracks changes in the world; principled understanding emerges when a model ceases to rely on memorized facts and discovers a compact "circuit" connecting these facts. Across these tiers, MI uncovers internal organizations that can underwrite understanding-like unification. However, these also diverge from human cognition in their parallel exploitation of heterogeneous mechanisms. Fusing philosophical theory with mechanistic evidence thus allows us to transcend binary debates over whether AI understands, paving the way for a comparative, mechanistically grounded epistemology that explores how AI understanding aligns with--and diverges from--our own.

papers.title: The Clock and the Pizza: Two Stories in Mechanistic Explanation of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Do neural networks, trained on well-understood algorithmic tasks, reliably re-discover known algorithms for solving those tasks, and under what conditions do they discover familiar algorithmic solutions?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on modular addition can discover qualitatively different algorithms (Clock, Pizza, and others), with the algorithm learned depending on hyperparameters like attention rate and width, revealing algorithmic phase transitions and the need for tools to characterize algorithmic phase spaces.
papers.conclusion: Algorithmic discoveries in neural networks are not inevitable; even simple tasks admit a diversity of solutions, motivating the development of tools to characterize the algorithmic phase space of neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Networks can learn either the previously described Clock algorithm or a new, less intuitive Pizza algorithm for modular addition.
The Pizza algorithm uses averaging and absolute value operations, while the Clock algorithm uses multiplication via attention.
Models sometimes implement multiple, parallel copies of an algorithm (ensembling) for robustness.
Sharp algorithmic phase transitions between Clock and Pizza occur as model hyperparameters (attention rate, width) are varied.
Non-circular algorithms also exist, especially in deeper networks or with low attention rates.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on a single learning problem (modular addition), and scaling the techniques to more complex models and real-world tasks requires significant additional work.
future_direction: How to find, classify, and interpret unfamiliar algorithms in a systematic way.
How to disentangle multiple, parallel algorithm implementations in the presence of ensembling.
papers.abstract: Do neural networks, trained on well-understood algorithmic tasks, reliably rediscover known algorithms for solving those tasks? Several recent studies, on tasks ranging from group arithmetic to in-context linear regression, have suggested that the answer is yes. Using modular addition as a prototypical problem, we show that algorithm discovery in neural networks is sometimes more complex. Small changes to model hyperparameters and initializations can induce the discovery of qualitatively different algorithms from a fixed training set, and even parallel implementations of multiple such algorithms. Some networks trained to perform modular addition implement a familiar Clock algorithm; others implement a previously undescribed, less intuitive, but comprehensible procedure which we term the Pizza algorithm, or a variety of even more complex procedures. Our results show that even simple learning problems can admit a surprising diversity of solutions, motivating the development of new tools for characterizing the behavior of neural networks across their algorithmic phase space.

papers.title: Dynamics Within Latent Chain-of-Thought: An Empirical Study of Causal Structure
papers.research_question: The paper investigates three key questions about latent chain-of-thought: (1) which steps are causally necessary for correctness and when answers become decidable early; (2) how influence propagates across steps and how this structure compares to explicit CoT; (3) whether intermediate trajectories retain competing answer modes and how output-level commitment differs from representational commitment across steps.
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides the first causal, step-resolved evaluation of latent CoT, showing that latent-step budgets function as staged interfaces with non-local routing and that there is a gap between early output bias and late representational commitment.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that latent-step budgets should be treated as an allocatable interface rather than homogeneous extra depth, and that improving latent reasoning requires shaping routing and commitment rather than simply adding more steps.
papers.key_findings:
Step-wise necessity is heterogeneous: intervening on different latent steps yields different flip rates, indicating unequal causal leverage.
Early-stop decoding shows that correctness becomes decodable at different steps for different tasks and models.
Influence propagation in latent CoT is non-local, with skip connections dominating, unlike explicit CoT which is more chain-like.
Intermediate latent trajectories can retain superposition of competing answer modes, with a gap between output-level commitment and representational commitment.
Coconut models show larger flip rates than CODI, and stronger backbones suppress flips but do not erase step-dependent patterns.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to single-step edits, a fixed latent budget (T=6), and a confined set of paradigms (Coconut/CODI), backbones, and benchmarks.
future_direction: Improving latent reasoning by explicitly shaping where information is written and how it is consolidated across steps (e.g., encouraging stable bottlenecks or controllable routing).
Broader evaluation across more paradigms, longer horizons, and varied intervention types.
papers.abstract: Latent or continuous chain-of-thought methods replace explicit textual rationales with a number of internal latent steps, but these intermediate computations are difficult to evaluate beyond correlation-based probes. In this paper, we view latent chain-of-thought as a manipulable causal process in representation space by modeling latent steps as variables in a structural causal model (SCM) and analyzing their effects through step-wise $\mathrm{do}$-interventions. We study two representative paradigms (i.e., Coconut and CODI) on both mathematical and general reasoning tasks to investigate three key questions: (1) which steps are causally necessary for correctness and when answers become decidable early; (2) how does influence propagate across steps, and how does this structure compare to explicit CoT; and (3) do intermediate trajectories retain competing answer modes, and how does output-level commitment differ from representational commitment across steps. We find that latent-step budgets behave less like homogeneous extra depth and more like staged functionality with non-local routing, and we identify a persistent gap between early output bias and late representational commitment. These results motivate mode-conditional and stability-aware analyses -- and corresponding training/decoding objectives -- as more reliable tools for interpreting and improving latent reasoning systems.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Scale for In-Context Learning: An Interpretability-based Case Study at 66 Billion Scale
papers.research_question: Are all LLM components really needed to perform in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Only a core nucleus of attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) in a large language model (OPT-66B) are important for in-context learning across a wide variety of tasks, and these important heads overlap with task-agnostic induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Large language models may be undertrained for in-context learning, and the findings motivate investigating pre-training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
~70% of attention heads and ~20% of FFNs can be removed with minimal decline in in-context learning task performance.
Important attention heads are primarily clustered in the intermediate layers of the model.
There is substantial overlap in the set of attention heads (un)important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples (shots).
A small set of attention heads in OPT-66B score highly on primitive induction operations (prefix matching and copying).
These induction heads overlap with task-specific important heads, indicating they are capable of more sophisticated in-context learning behaviors.
papers.limitation:
No causal link is claimed between induction heads and sophisticated in-context learning capabilities; deeper investigation is needed.
The study uses only up to 5 in-context examples and random selection of examples.
All downstream tasks are monolingual.
future_direction: Increase the number and strength of induction heads via auxiliary pre-training objectives for primitives like prefix matching and copying.
Investigate and improve (pre-)training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
Replicate the study with instruction-tuned model variants (e.g., OPT-IML).
papers.abstract: Hritik Bansal, Karthik Gopalakrishnan, Saket Dingliwal, Sravan Bodapati, Katrin Kirchhoff, Dan Roth. Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2023.

papers.title: Diagnosing Pathological Chain-of-Thought in Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is fundamental to modern LLM architectures and represents a critical intervention point for AI safety. However, CoT reasoning may exhibit failure modes that we note as pathologies, which prevent it from being useful for monitoring. Prior work has identified three distinct pathologies: post-hoc rationalization, where models generate plausible explanations backwards from predetermined answers; encoded reasoning, where intermediate steps conceal information within seemingly interpretable text; and internalized reasoning, where models replace explicit reasoning with meaningless filler tokens while computing internally. To better understand and discriminate between these pathologies, we create a set of concrete metrics that are simple to implement, computationally inexpensive, and task-agnostic. To validate our approach, we develop model organisms deliberately trained to exhibit specific CoT pathologies. Our work provides a practical toolkit for assessing CoT pathologies, with direct implications for training-time monitoring.

papers.title: The Potential of CoT for Reasoning: A Closer Look at Trace Dynamics
papers.research_question: How do different parts of chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning contribute to the final answer in large language models, and what patterns can be observed in the dynamics of CoT traces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the 'potential' metric to quantify the contribution of different parts of chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, revealing patterns like non-monotonicity, insights, jumps, and tangents, and shows that partial CoT from stronger models can significantly improve weaker models' performance.
papers.conclusion: The potential metric provides a useful lens for understanding CoT reasoning, revealing interpretable patterns and transferable insights, and could be used for future analysis and reward design in RL.
papers.key_findings:
The potential of CoT often exhibits strong non-monotonicity due to reasoning tangents.
Sharp spikes in potential correspond to reasoning insights and jumps, some of which are interpretable while others are not.
Models sometimes arrive at correct answers through lucky guesses without relevant justifications.
As little as 20% of partial CoT from a stronger model can unlock the performance of a weaker model on previously unsolvable problems.
CoT mechanisms are transferable between different models, even across model families.
papers.limitation:
The computational complexity of calculating the potential and generating optimal CoT is high, limiting practical use.
Some spikes in the potential are difficult to interpret from a human perspective.
future_direction: Using potential to pin-point important parts in long CoT chains
Using potential as a partial reward in RL training for fine-grained credit assignment
Leveraging transferability of partial CoTs in reinforcement learning to reduce reward sparsity
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting is a de-facto standard technique to elicit reasoning-like responses from large language models (LLMs), allowing them to spell out individual steps before giving a final answer. While the resemblance to human-like reasoning is undeniable, the driving forces underpinning the success of CoT reasoning still remain largely unclear. In this work, we perform an in-depth analysis of CoT traces originating from competition-level mathematics questions, with the aim of better understanding how, and which parts of CoT actually contribute to the final answer. To this end, we introduce the notion of a potential, quantifying how much a given part of CoT increases the likelihood of a correct completion. Upon examination of reasoning traces through the lens of the potential, we identify surprising patterns including (1) its often strong non-monotonicity (due to reasoning tangents), (2) very sharp but sometimes tough to interpret spikes (reasoning insights and jumps) as well as (3) at times lucky guesses, where the model arrives at the correct answer without providing any relevant justifications before. While some of the behaviours of the potential are readily interpretable and align with human intuition (such as insights and tangents), others remain difficult to understand from a human perspective. To further quantify the reliance of LLMs on reasoning insights, we investigate the notion of CoT transferability, where we measure the potential of a weaker model under the partial CoT from another, stronger model. Indeed aligning with our previous results, we find that as little as 20% of partial CoT can ``unlock'' the performance of the weaker model on problems that were previously unsolvable for it, highlighting that a large part of the mechanics underpinning CoT are transferable.

papers.title: Distilled Circuits: A Mechanistic Study of Internal Restructuring in Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge distillation restructure internal circuits and representations in student models, and how can functional alignment between teacher and student be quantified?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic understanding of how knowledge distillation restructures internal circuits, showing that students compress and discard teacher components, and introduces an alignment metric to quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity.
papers.conclusion: While student models preserve broad functional behavior from their teachers, knowledge distillation causes significant internal circuit restructuring, leading to increased reliance on fewer components and reduced robustness. The alignment metric captures functional similarity beyond output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, leading to stronger reliance on fewer components.
Student models are more vulnerable to component ablation, indicating reduced robustness.
The introduced alignment metric effectively quantifies functional alignment between teacher and student models.
These findings on internal restructuring and reduced robustness generalize across different model architectures (GPT2, BERT, Llama).
Performance similarity does not guarantee similarity in internal computation; circuit-level analysis is essential for understanding functional alignment.
papers.limitation:
The study is constrained by the relatively small set of models evaluated (6).
The component role attribution procedure is manual and could be automated.
The alignment metric could be improved in granularity and interpretability.
The findings are based on specific tasks and models and may not generalize to all settings.
future_direction: Apply the methodology and alignment metric to a broader, more diverse collection of models.
Automate the component role attribution procedure, potentially using interpretability agents.
Improve the alignment metric's granularity and interpretability, and explore incorporating it as a loss term during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses a larger neural model (teacher) into smaller, faster student models by training them to match teacher outputs. However, the internal computational transformations that occur during this process remain poorly understood. We apply techniques from mechanistic interpretability to analyze how internal circuits, representations, and activation patterns differ between teacher and student. Focusing on GPT2-small and its distilled counterpart DistilGPT2, we find that student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, often resulting in stronger reliance on fewer individual components. To quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity, we introduce an alignment metric based on influence-weighted component similarity, validated across multiple tasks. Our findings reveal that while knowledge distillation preserves broad functional behaviors, it also causes significant shifts in internal computation, with important implications for the robustness and generalization capacity of distilled models.

papers.title: Dissociation of Faithful and Unfaithful Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do LLMs recover from errors in Chain of Thought, and what factors affect faithful versus unfaithful recovery?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that LLMs have two distinct modes of reasoning (faithful and unfaithful) when recovering from errors in chain-of-thought, and these modes respond differently to factors like error magnitude and context.
papers.conclusion: LLMs have two distinct reasoning modes: one faithful and interpretable, and one unfaithful where the generated text does not accurately represent the internal reasoning. This challenges the reliability of chain-of-thought for model auditing.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs recover more frequently from larger errors than smaller ones.
Prior expectations of errors (via context noise or prompting) increase error recovery rates.
More evidence for the correct value in the context increases error recovery rates.
Faithful and unfaithful recoveries respond differently to interventions, indicating distinct mechanisms.
Different models (GPT-4, Claude-3 Opus, Llama-3) show varying patterns in faithful vs. unfaithful recovery.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to mathematical reasoning problems and does not investigate non-mathematical reasoning errors; additionally, the introduced errors may differ from naturally occurring errors.
future_direction: Understanding the mechanisms underlying faithful and unfaithful reasoning modes
Identifying factors that influence which reasoning mode is activated
Developing techniques to encourage faithful reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often improve their performance in downstream tasks when they generate Chain of Thought reasoning text before producing an answer. We investigate how LLMs recover from errors in Chain of Thought. Through analysis of error recovery behaviors, we find evidence for unfaithfulness in Chain of Thought, which occurs when models arrive at the correct answer despite invalid reasoning text. We identify factors that shift LLM recovery behavior: LLMs recover more frequently from obvious errors and in contexts that provide more evidence for the correct answer. Critically, these factors have divergent effects on faithful and unfaithful recoveries. Our results indicate that there are distinct mechanisms driving faithful and unfaithful error recoveries. Selective targeting of these mechanisms may be able to drive down the rate of unfaithful reasoning and improve model interpretability.

papers.title: Schoenfeld's Anatomy of Mathematical Reasoning by Language Models
papers.research_question: Do reasoning traces exhibit consistent structure when abstracted into functional episodes? How do reasoning dynamics differ across models? How do episode patterns correlate with correctness and efficiency?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ThinkARM, a framework for abstracting reasoning traces into functional episodes, enabling systematic analysis of reasoning structure and dynamics in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Episode-level representations make reasoning steps explicit, enabling systematic analysis of how reasoning is structured, stabilized, and altered in modern language models.
papers.key_findings:
Episode-level analysis reveals a functional progression from abstract reasoning to concrete execution to evaluative control.
Reasoning models distribute effort across analysis, exploration, execution, and verification, while non-reasoning models are heavily execution-focused.
Exploration serves as a critical branching point: correct solutions route exploration into monitoring or re-analysis, while incorrect ones tend to continue execution or terminate.
Efficient reasoning methods selectively suppress evaluation-oriented episodes and feedback loops, diverging from base model patterns.
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly expose reasoning traces, yet their underlying cognitive structure and steps remain difficult to identify and analyze beyond surface-level statistics. We adopt Schoenfeld's Episode Theory as an inductive, intermediate-scale lens and introduce ThinkARM (Anatomy of Reasoning in Models), a scalable framework that explicitly abstracts reasoning traces into functional reasoning steps such as Analysis, Explore, Implement, Verify, etc. When applied to mathematical problem solving by diverse models, this abstraction reveals reproducible thinking dynamics and structural differences between reasoning and non-reasoning models, which are not apparent from token-level views. We further present two diagnostic case studies showing that exploration functions as a critical branching step associated with correctness, and that efficiency-oriented methods selectively suppress evaluative feedback steps rather than uniformly shortening responses. Together, our results demonstrate that episode-level representations make reasoning steps explicit, enabling systematic analysis of how reasoning is structured, stabilized, and altered in modern language models.

papers.title: Selective Induction Heads: How Transformers Select Causal Structures In Context
papers.research_question: How do transformers select causal structures in context? Specifically, how can they dynamically handle causal structures that change with context?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for selective induction heads, showing how transformers can learn to select the correct causal structure in-context for next-token prediction in interleaved Markov chains.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance the understanding of how transformers select causal structures, providing new insights into their functioning and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers learn selective induction heads to dynamically select the correct causal structure in-context.
A 3-layer attention-only transformer can implement the selective induction head mechanism.
The constructed transformer matches the performance of trained transformers.
The mechanism asymptotically converges to the maximum likelihood solution.
papers.abstract: Transformers have exhibited exceptional capabilities in sequence modeling tasks, leveraging self-attention and in-context learning. Critical to this success are induction heads, attention circuits that enable copying tokens based on their previous occurrences. In this work, we introduce a novel framework that showcases transformers' ability to dynamically handle causal structures. Existing works rely on Markov Chains to study the formation of induction heads, revealing how transformers capture causal dependencies and learn transition probabilities in-context. However, they rely on a fixed causal structure that fails to capture the complexity of natural languages, where the relationship between tokens dynamically changes with context. To this end, our framework varies the causal structure through interleaved Markov chains with different lags while keeping the transition probabilities fixed. This setting unveils the formation of Selective Induction Heads, a new circuit that endows transformers with the ability to select the correct causal structure in-context. We empirically demonstrate that transformers learn this mechanism to predict the next token by identifying the correct lag and copying the corresponding token from the past. We provide a detailed construction of a 3-layer transformer to implement the selective induction head, and a theoretical analysis proving that this mechanism asymptotically converges to the maximum likelihood solution. Our findings advance the understanding of how transformers select causal structures, providing new insights into their functioning and interpretability.

papers.title: Visual Thoughts: A Unified Perspective of Understanding Multimodal Chain-of-Thought
papers.research_question: Is there a unified explanation for why different multimodal chain-of-thought paradigms enhance large vision-language models in distinct ways?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning improves large vision-language models by incorporating visual thoughts, which act as an intermediate cache for visual information, enabling more efficient and effective reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Visual thoughts provide a unified perspective for understanding how multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning enhances large vision-language models, acting as visual caches that improve information flow and reasoning performance.
papers.key_findings:
Removing visual thoughts from the reasoning process impairs model performance more than reasoning directly from the query alone.
Different expressions of visual thoughts (natural language, structured language, edited image, generative image) vary in effectiveness depending on task clarity and conciseness.
Visual thoughts serve as primary intermediaries, connecting input images to deeper transformer layers and facilitating advanced visual information processing.
Image-form visual thoughts consistently outperform text-form visual thoughts, especially in complex scenarios requiring detailed visual information.
Visual thoughts are more effective than simple image captions for conveying visual information in complex scenes, improving reasoning accuracy.
future_direction: Exploring the integration of multiple visual thoughts to enhance visual information transmission in multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have achieved significant success in multimodal tasks, with multimodal chain-of-thought (MCoT) further enhancing performance and interpretability. Recent MCoT methods fall into two categories: (i) Textual-MCoT (T-MCoT), which takes multimodal input and produces textual output; and (ii) Interleaved-MCoT (I-MCoT), which generates interleaved image-text outputs. Despite advances in both approaches, the mechanisms driving these improvements are not fully understood. To fill this gap, we first reveal that MCoT boosts LVLMs by incorporating visual thoughts, which convey image information to the reasoning process regardless of the MCoT format, depending only on clarity and conciseness of expression. Furthermore, to explore visual thoughts systematically, we define four distinct forms of visual thought expressions and analyze them comprehensively. Our findings demonstrate that these forms differ in clarity and conciseness, yielding varying levels of MCoT improvement. Additionally, we explore the internal nature of visual thoughts, finding that visual thoughts serve as intermediaries between the input image and reasoning to deeper transformer layers, enabling more advanced visual information transmission. We hope that the visual thoughts can inspire further breakthroughs for future MCoT research.

papers.title: Adaptive Circuit Behavior and Generalization in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How well does the indirect object identification (IOI) circuit in GPT-2 small generalize to prompt variants that challenge the assumptions of its algorithm?
papers.core_contribution: The IOI circuit generalizes surprisingly well to prompt variants, reusing all its components and mechanisms while only adding additional input edges, and a mechanism called S2 Hacking explains how the circuit outperforms the full model on these variants.
papers.conclusion: The IOI circuit in GPT-2 small generalizes more effectively than previously understood, reusing its core components and mechanisms while adapting through minimal structural changes, offering insights into the broader capabilities of large neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
The base IOI circuit outperforms the full model on DoubleIO and TripleIO prompt variants where the IOI algorithm would fail.
A mechanism termed S2 Hacking explains how the circuit achieves high performance on these variants by focusing on the S2 token due to the knockout procedure.
New circuits discovered for DoubleIO and TripleIO variants reuse all components of the base IOI circuit, only adding edges from additional input tokens (IO2 for DoubleIO, IO2 and IO3 for TripleIO).
The circuit components (attention heads) largely retain their functionalities from the base IOI task when evaluated on the variants.
The order of names in the prompt affects performance, with a 'first come, first serve' mechanism observed in a Previous Token head (2.2).
future_direction: a more detailed study of the duplicate suppression mechanism
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the inner workings of large neural networks by identifying circuits, or minimal subgraphs within the model that implement algorithms responsible for performing specific tasks. These circuits are typically discovered and analyzed using a narrowly defined prompt format. However, given the abilities of large language models (LLMs) to generalize across various prompt formats for the same task, it remains unclear how well these circuits generalize. For instance, it is unclear whether the models generalization results from reusing the same circuit components, the components behaving differently, or the use of entirely different components. In this paper, we investigate the generality of the indirect object identification (IOI) circuit in GPT-2 small, which is well-studied and believed to implement a simple, interpretable algorithm. We evaluate its performance on prompt variants that challenge the assumptions of this algorithm. Our findings reveal that the circuit generalizes surprisingly well, reusing all of its components and mechanisms while only adding additional input edges. Notably, the circuit generalizes even to prompt variants where the original algorithm should fail; we discover a mechanism that explains this which we term S2 Hacking. Our findings indicate that circuits within LLMs may be more flexible and general than previously recognized, underscoring the importance of studying circuit generalization to better understand the broader capabilities of these models.

papers.title: Emergence of Minimal Circuits for Indirect Object Identification in Attention-Only Transformers
papers.research_question: How do minimal circuits for indirect object identification emerge in attention-only transformers trained from scratch on a symbolic task?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that task-constrained training induces highly interpretable, minimal circuits for indirect object identification in attention-only transformers.
papers.conclusion: Task-constrained training can produce parsimonious and interpretable circuits, offering insight into computational motifs underlying reasoning in larger models.
papers.key_findings:
A single-layer, two-head attention-only transformer achieves perfect accuracy on the symbolic IOI task.
The two heads specialize into additive and contrastive subcircuits that jointly implement IOI resolution.
A two-layer, one-head model achieves similar performance through composition across layers via query-value interactions.
Positional embeddings improve accuracy and interpretability but are not strictly necessary for the task.
The circuits in task-constrained models are more parsimonious than those in broadly pre-trained models.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer large language models (LLMs) into human-understandable computational circuits. However, the complexity of pretrained models often obscures the minimal mechanisms required for specific reasoning tasks. In this work, we train small, attention-only transformers from scratch on a symbolic version of the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task -- a benchmark for studying coreference -- like reasoning in transformers. Surprisingly, a single-layer model with only two attention heads achieves perfect IOI accuracy, despite lacking MLPs and normalization layers. Through residual stream decomposition, spectral analysis, and embedding interventions, we find that the two heads specialize into additive and contrastive subcircuits that jointly implement IOI resolution. Furthermore, we show that a two-layer, one-head model achieves similar performance by composing information across layers through query-value interactions. These results demonstrate that task-specific training induces highly interpretable, minimal circuits, offering a controlled testbed for probing the computational foundations of transformer reasoning.

papers.title: Reasoning with Latent Thoughts: On the Power of Looped Transformers
papers.research_question: Does reasoning require large depth but not necessarily many parameters, and can looped models effectively solve reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Looped transformers can solve reasoning tasks with fewer parameters by providing depth through looping, and they exhibit an inductive bias towards reasoning over memorization.
papers.conclusion: Looped models are effective for reasoning tasks, providing depth without many parameters, and have an inductive bias towards improving reasoning performance over memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Looped models nearly match the performance of non-looped models with the same depth on synthetic reasoning tasks like addition, p-hop induction, and i-GSM, despite having fewer parameters.
For language modeling, looped models have worse perplexity but better reasoning performance on downstream tasks compared to non-looped models with the same FLOPs.
Looped models show scaling behavior with effective depth similar to chain-of-thought reasoning.
Theoretically, looped models can simulate iterative algorithms and chain-of-thought reasoning.
A regularization method that encourages layer similarity inherits the inductive bias of looped models towards reasoning.
papers.limitation: The results are limited to the tested reasoning problems and may not generalize to other forms of reasoning (e.g., multimodal and common-sense reasoning).
future_direction: Generalizing the results to other forms of reasoning such as multimodal and common-sense reasoning.
Formalizing reasoning problems more succinctly.
Further exploration of the inductive bias towards reasoning at the same perplexity.
papers.abstract: Large language models have shown remarkable reasoning abilities and scaling laws suggest that large parameter count, especially along the depth axis, is the primary driver. In this work, we make a stronger claim -- many reasoning problems require a large depth but not necessarily many parameters. This unlocks a novel application of looped models for reasoning. Firstly, we show that for many synthetic reasoning problems like addition, $p$-hop induction, and math problems, a $k$-layer transformer looped $L$ times nearly matches the performance of a $kL$-layer non-looped model, and is significantly better than a $k$-layer model. This is further corroborated by theoretical results showing that many such reasoning problems can be solved via iterative algorithms, and thus, can be solved effectively using looped models with nearly optimal depth. Perhaps surprisingly, these benefits also translate to practical settings of language modeling -- on many downstream reasoning tasks, a language model with $k$-layers looped $L$ times can be competitive to, if not better than, a $kL$-layer language model. In fact, our empirical analysis reveals an intriguing phenomenon: looped and non-looped models exhibit scaling behavior that depends on their effective depth, akin to the inference-time scaling of chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. We further elucidate the connection to CoT reasoning by proving that looped models implicitly generate latent thoughts and can simulate $T$ steps of CoT with $T$ loops. Inspired by these findings, we also present an interesting dichotomy between reasoning and memorization, and design a looping-based regularization that is effective on both fronts.

papers.title: Beyond Semantics: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Reasonless Intermediate Tokens
papers.research_question: What is the role of end-user semantics of derivational traces (intermediate tokens) in transformer models? Specifically, is the semantic meaning of intermediate tokens necessary for model performance?
papers.core_contribution: Intermediate tokens (reasoning traces) do not need to be semantically meaningful to improve model performance, and trace validity does not strongly correlate with solution correctness.
papers.conclusion: Intermediate tokens do not have end-user interpretability/semantics, and if the goal is to increase model performance, enforcing trace semantics is unnecessary and potentially misleading.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained on corrupted (semantically irrelevant) traces achieve performance comparable to, and sometimes exceeding, models trained on correct traces.
There is a weak correlation between solution correctness and the validity of the reasoning trace that precedes it; models often produce correct solutions from invalid traces.
Post-training with reinforcement learning (GRPO) improves solution accuracy but does not consistently enhance trace validity.
The length of generated reasoning traces is largely agnostic to the underlying computational complexity of the problem being solved.
Models trained on corrupted traces generalize better on out-of-distribution tasks than models trained on correct traces.
papers.abstract: Recent impressive results from large reasoning models have been interpreted as a triumph of Chain of Thought (CoT), especially of training on CoTs sampled from base LLMs to help find new reasoning patterns. While these traces certainly seem to help model performance, it is not clear how they actually influence it, with some works ascribing semantics to the traces and others cautioning against relying on them as transparent and faithful proxies of the model's internal computational process. To systematically investigate the role of end-user semantics of derivational traces, we set up a controlled study where we train transformer models from scratch on formally verifiable reasoning traces and the solutions they lead to. We notice that, despite significant gains over the solution-only baseline, models trained on entirely correct traces can still produce invalid reasoning traces even when arriving at correct solutions. More interestingly, our experiments also show that models trained on corrupted traces, whose intermediate reasoning steps bear no relation to the problem they accompany, perform similarly to those trained on correct ones, and even generalize better on out-of-distribution tasks. We also study the effect of GRPO-based RL post-training on trace validity, noting that while solution accuracy increase, this is not accompanied by any improvements in trace validity. Finally, we examine whether reasoning-trace length reflects inference-time scaling and find that trace length is largely agnostic to the underlying computational complexity of the problem being solved. These results challenge the assumption that intermediate tokens or ``Chains of Thought'' reflect or induce predictable reasoning behaviors and caution against anthropomorphizing such outputs or over-interpreting them (despite their mostly seemingly forms) as evidence of human-like or algorithmic behaviors in language models.

papers.title: Reason to Rote: Rethinking Memorization in Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do language models memorize label noise, and why does such memorization not heavily affect generalizable reasoning capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Memorization of noisy labels in language models builds on, rather than overrides, the underlying reasoning mechanisms, with memories stored via distributed encoding and outlier heuristics in neurons.
papers.conclusion: The findings show that memorization of label noise builds on existing reasoning mechanisms, using distributed encoding and outlier heuristics, explaining the phenomenon of benign memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Models first learn to generalize on noisy training instances (predicting correct labels) before memorizing the noisy labels.
Even when producing memorized noisy labels, models continue to compute intermediate reasoning outputs corresponding to the correct labels.
Memorization and generalization circuits substantially overlap, indicating memorization builds on existing generalization mechanisms.
Memorization uses distributed encoding across multiple input tokens and intermediate results rather than a simple lookup.
In the FDA task, memorization occurs via 'outlier heuristics' where higher-layer MLP neurons slightly shift their activation patterns to fit noisy labels.
papers.limitation:
Focus on relatively small language models; larger models might exhibit different behaviors.
Models trained from scratch, so influence of pretraining data is not considered.
Examination of implicit reasoning without explicit solution steps; not studying models with explicit chain-of-thought.
future_direction: Study memorization in larger models
Investigate effect of pretraining on memorization and reasoning
Study memorization in models with explicit chain-of-thought reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models readily memorize arbitrary training instances, such as label noise, yet they perform strikingly well on reasoning tasks. In this work, we investigate how language models memorize label noise, and why such memorization in many cases does not heavily affect generalizable reasoning capabilities. Using two controllable synthetic reasoning datasets with noisy labels, four-digit addition (FDA) and two-hop relational reasoning (THR), we discover a reliance of memorization on generalizable reasoning mechanisms: models continue to compute intermediate reasoning outputs even when retrieving memorized noisy labels, and intervening reasoning adversely affects memorization. We further show that memorization operates through distributed encoding, i.e., aggregating various inputs and intermediate results, rather than building a look-up mechanism from inputs to noisy labels. Moreover, our FDA case study reveals memorization occurs via outlier heuristics, where existing neuron activation patterns are slightly shifted to fit noisy labels. Together, our findings suggest that memorization of label noise in language models builds on, rather than overrides, the underlying reasoning mechanisms, shedding lights on the intriguing phenomenon of benign memorization.

papers.title: Birth of a Transformer: A Memory Viewpoint
papers.research_question: How do transformers balance global knowledge and in-context learning during training, specifically in the development of induction head mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a synthetic bigram dataset and an associative memory viewpoint to study learning dynamics in two-layer transformers, showing that induction heads emerge through top-down gradient-based learning.
papers.conclusion: The associative memory viewpoint provides valuable insights into transformer learning dynamics, offering a foundation for better interpretability and improvements in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Global bigram associations are learned rapidly, while in-context induction mechanisms develop more slowly.
Transformer weight matrices can be viewed as associative memories that store input-output embedding pairs.
The induction head mechanism forms in a top-down manner, with output matrices learning before key-query matrices.
Theoretical gradient analysis shows how associative memories are recovered from noisy inputs during training.
Data distribution properties, such as trigger frequency and output uniformity, affect the learning speed and accuracy of associative memories.
papers.limitation:
The simplified transformer architecture lacks components like non-linear MLPs, multiple heads, and layer normalization, which are present in standard transformers.
The synthetic dataset may not fully capture the complexity of real-world language data.
future_direction: Extending the associative memory viewpoint to non-linear components and multi-head architectures.
Applying insights to optimization algorithms, data selection, and model editing for LLMs.
Studying how such mechanisms scale to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models based on transformers have achieved great empirical successes. However, as they are deployed more widely, there is a growing need to better understand their internal mechanisms in order to make them more reliable. These models appear to store vast amounts of knowledge from their training data, and to adapt quickly to new information provided in their context or prompt. We study how transformers balance these two types of knowledge by considering a synthetic setup where tokens are generated from either global or context-specific bigram distributions. By a careful empirical analysis of the training process on a simplified two-layer transformer, we illustrate the fast learning of global bigrams and the slower development of an "induction head" mechanism for the in-context bigrams. We highlight the role of weight matrices as associative memories, provide theoretical insights on how gradients enable their learning during training, and study the role of data-distributional properties.

papers.title: In-Context Language Learning: Architectures and Algorithms
papers.research_question: Which model classes can perform in-context language learning (ICLL), what algorithmic solutions do they implement, and how can architectural changes improve ICLL?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces in-context language learning (ICLL) as a model problem for studying ICL, shows Transformers outperform other models by implementing n-gram heads, and demonstrates that adding n-gram heads improves ICLL and natural language modeling.
papers.conclusion: ICLL is a useful model problem for understanding ICL, and n-gram heads are a key mechanism in Transformers for ICLL that can be used to improve other models.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers significantly outperform recurrent and convolutional models on ICLL tasks.
Transformers develop specialized n-gram heads (higher-order induction heads) to compute in-context n-gram statistics.
Probing shows that Transformers better encode n-gram counts in hidden states compared to other models.
Hard-wiring n-gram heads into other models (RNNs, convolutional) improves their ICLL performance.
Adding n-gram heads also improves natural language modeling perplexity.
papers.limitation: Many aspects of ICLL, even with regular languages, remain to be understood (e.g. learning dynamics and out-of-distribution generalization).
future_direction: Extend ICLL to more expressive languages (context-free or context-sensitive)
Extend experiments to larger models trained with more tokens
papers.abstract: Large-scale neural language models exhibit a remarkable capacity for in-context learning (ICL): they can infer novel functions from datasets provided as input. Most of our current understanding of when and how ICL arises comes from LMs trained on extremely simple learning problems like linear regression and associative recall. There remains a significant gap between these model problems and the "real" ICL exhibited by LMs trained on large text corpora, which involves not just retrieval and function approximation but free-form generation of language and other structured outputs. In this paper, we study ICL through the lens of a new family of model problems we term in context language learning (ICLL). In ICLL, LMs are presented with a set of strings from a formal language, and must generate additional strings from the same language. We focus on in-context learning of regular languages generated by random finite automata. We evaluate a diverse set of neural sequence models (including several RNNs, Transformers, and state-space model variants) on regular ICLL tasks, aiming to answer three questions: (1) Which model classes are empirically capable of ICLL? (2) What algorithmic solutions do successful models implement to perform ICLL? (3) What architectural changes can improve ICLL in less performant models? We first show that Transformers significantly outperform neural sequence models with recurrent or convolutional representations on ICLL tasks. Next, we provide evidence that their ability to do so relies on specialized "n-gram heads" (higher-order variants of induction heads) that compute input-conditional next-token distributions. Finally, we show that hard-wiring these heads into neural models improves performance not just on ICLL, but natural language modeling -- improving the perplexity of 340M-parameter models by up to 1.14 points (6.7%) on the SlimPajama dataset.

papers.title: Are formal and functional linguistic mechanisms dissociated in language models?
papers.research_question: Do current large language models exhibit distinct localization (dissociation) of formal and functional linguistic mechanisms in their internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds evidence for formal-functional dissociation in LLMs in terms of cross-task faithfulness (formal task circuits perform other formal tasks better than functional ones, and vice-versa), but not in terms of circuit overlap, suggesting a shared pool of mechanisms for formal tasks rather than a single unified region.
papers.conclusion: There is evidence for emerging formal-functional dissociation in LLMs in terms of cross-task faithfulness, but not in terms of circuit overlap, indicating a set of shared formal linguistic mechanisms rather than a single unified region.
papers.key_findings:
Circuits for formal and functional linguistic tasks have low overlap (IoU).
Circuits for formal tasks do not have especially high overlap with each other, arguing against a single unified formal network.
Formal task circuits perform other formal tasks better than they perform functional tasks (cross-task faithfulness).
Functional task circuits perform other functional tasks better than they perform formal tasks (cross-task faithfulness).
Clustering based on cross-task faithfulness vectors separates formal and functional tasks into distinct groups.
papers.limitation: The circuit-finding method (EAP-IG) may not perfectly capture all relevant mechanisms, and the findings are limited to the specific models and tasks studied.
future_direction: Studying more models and tasks to generalize findings.
Using more granular analyses (e.g., neuron-level, sparse feature circuits).
Investigating the effects of model scale and architecture on dissociation.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable, these capabilities are unevenly distributed: they excel at formal linguistic tasks, such as producing fluent, grammatical text, but struggle more with functional linguistic tasks like reasoning and consistent fact retrieval. Inspired by neuroscience, recent work suggests that to succeed on both formal and functional linguistic tasks, LLMs should use different mechanisms for each; such localization could either be built-in or emerge spontaneously through training. In this paper, we ask: do current models, with fast-improving functional linguistic abilities, exhibit distinct localization of formal and functional linguistic mechanisms? We answer this by finding and comparing the "circuits", or minimal computational subgraphs, responsible for various formal and functional tasks. Comparing 5 LLMs across 10 distinct tasks, we find that while there is indeed little overlap between circuits for formal and functional tasks, there is also little overlap between formal linguistic tasks, as exists in the human brain. Thus, a single formal linguistic network, unified and distinct from functional task circuits, remains elusive. However, in terms of cross-task faithfulness - the ability of one circuit to solve another's task - we observe a separation between formal and functional mechanisms, suggesting that shared mechanisms between formal tasks may exist.

papers.title: DeCoT: Debiasing Chain-of-Thought for Knowledge-Intensive Tasks in Large Language Models via Causal Intervention
papers.research_question: How does internal knowledge bias in large language models impair chain-of-thought reasoning, and how can this bias be mitigated via causal intervention?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a causal view to explain internal knowledge bias in LLMs and introduces DeCoT, a method that uses external knowledge as an instrumental variable and front-door adjustment to debias chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.conclusion: DeCoT effectively alleviates the spurious correlation caused by internal knowledge bias, enabling LLMs to generate more accurate and logically sound chain-of-thought reasoning and final answers.
papers.key_findings:
Internal knowledge bias in LLMs can trigger the use of irrelevant information in prompts, leading to incoherent reasoning chains that impair logical reasoning.
DeCoT, by estimating the average causal effect (ACE) of CoT paths and sampling CoTs with high ACE, effectively reduces spurious correlation and improves reasoning accuracy.
The method consistently improves performance across multiple knowledge-intensive tasks and LLM backbones compared to standard CoT and context-aware contrastive decoding baselines.
DeCoT is compatible with and can improve other reasoning frameworks like ReAct by incorporating counterfactual debiasing.
The number of selected entities and alternative entities for causal intervention impacts performance, with more entities generally leading to better results but at increased computational cost.
papers.limitation: As an inference-stage causal intervention method, the improvement is limited by the upper bound of the LLM's capacity.
future_direction: Incorporate unbiased causal learning methods in the model pretraining or instruction tuning stage for more robust CoT reasoning.
Study the theoretical causal foundation of CoT prompting's mediator role in LLMs for better interpretability.
papers.abstract: Junda Wu, Tong Yu, Xiang Chen, Haoliang Wang, Ryan Rossi, Sungchul Kim, Anup Rao, Julian McAuley. Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

papers.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
papers.research_question: Do circuit analyses of LLMs generalize across training time and model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Circuit analyses are consistent across training and scale: task abilities and supporting functional components emerge at similar token counts across model sizes, and the overarching algorithms implemented by circuits remain stable even when individual components change.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analyses generalize well over both training and scale, suggesting that studies on small models at the end of pre-training can inform understanding of larger models and models with longer training.
papers.key_findings:
Task abilities and functional components (e.g., induction heads, name-mover heads) emerge consistently at similar token counts across different model scales.
The algorithm implemented by a circuit remains stable over training even when the specific attention heads implementing it change.
Circuit size correlates with model size and can fluctuate over time while the algorithm remains the same.
Components like induction heads emerge around 2B tokens across scales, paralleling task learning curves.
Circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training provide insights that generalize to larger models and longer training runs.
papers.limitation:
The study does not include fine-tuning or other post-training techniques.
Circuit completeness is challenging to verify.
The findings need validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
future_direction: Validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
Investigating the load-balancing mechanism that maintains task performance when components change.
papers.abstract: Most currently deployed large language models (LLMs) undergo continuous training or additional finetuning. By contrast, most research into LLMs' internal mechanisms focuses on models at one snapshot in time (the end of pre-training), raising the question of whether their results generalize to real-world settings. Existing studies of mechanisms over time focus on encoder-only or toy models, which differ significantly from most deployed models. In this study, we track how model mechanisms, operationalized as circuits, emerge and evolve across 300 billion tokens of training in decoder-only LLMs, in models ranging from 70 million to 2.8 billion parameters. We find that task abilities and the functional components that support them emerge consistently at similar token counts across scale. Moreover, although such components may be implemented by different attention heads over time, the overarching algorithm that they implement remains. Surprisingly, both these algorithms and the types of components involved therein can replicate across model scale. These results suggest that circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training can provide insights that still apply after additional pre-training and over model scale.

papers.title: Induction Heads as an Essential Mechanism for Pattern Matching in In-context Learning
papers.research_question: What is the role of induction heads in few-shot in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides empirical evidence that induction heads, through their prefix matching and copying mechanism, are a fundamental component enabling few-shot in-context learning in large language models.
papers.conclusion: Induction heads are a fundamental mechanism underlying in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating a small percentage (1-3%) of induction heads leads to substantial decreases in ICL performance, much more so than ablating random heads.
Blocking the specific induction attention pattern (via attention knockout) causes performance drops similar to full head ablation, confirming the mechanism's specific role.
The importance of induction heads for ICL holds across abstract pattern recognition tasks and real-world NLP tasks.
Induction heads utilize a 'fuzzy' version of the prefix matching and copying mechanism to enable pattern matching in ICL.
The ablation of induction heads affects few-shot performance more severely than zero-shot performance, highlighting their role in learning from examples.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on prefix-matching scores as a proxy for identifying induction heads, lacking a mechanistic basis for definitive identification.
Attention knockout experiments are confined to abstract-pattern recognition tasks; further research is required for NLP tasks.
The experiments do not test whether induction heads are the only computational process contributing to ICL; other mechanisms may exist.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown a remarkable ability to learn and perform complex tasks through in-context learning (ICL). However, a comprehensive understanding of its internal mechanisms is still lacking. This paper explores the role of induction heads in a few-shot ICL setting. We analyse two state-of-the-art models, Llama-3-8B and InternLM2-20B on abstract pattern recognition and NLP tasks. Our results show that even a minimal ablation of induction heads leads to ICL performance decreases of up to ~32% for abstract pattern recognition tasks, bringing the performance close to random. For NLP tasks, this ablation substantially decreases the model's ability to benefit from examples, bringing few-shot ICL performance close to that of zero-shot prompts. We further use attention knockout to disable specific induction patterns, and present fine-grained evidence for the role that the induction mechanism plays in ICL.

papers.title: A Toy Model of Universality: Reverse Engineering How Networks Learn Group Operations
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the universality hypothesis: whether different models learn similar features and circuits when trained on similar tasks, by studying how small neural networks learn to implement group composition.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the group composition via representations (GCR) algorithm and shows that neural networks consistently learn this algorithm when trained on group composition tasks, providing evidence for weak universality (underlying principles exist) but against strong universality (specific circuits vary).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that while there is an underlying algorithm (GCR) that networks learn for group composition, the specific features and circuits are arbitrary, supporting weak universality but not strong universality.
papers.key_findings:
Networks learn the GCR algorithm for group composition, which uses representation theory to compute compositions.
The specific representations (circuits) learned vary across different runs and hyperparameters, indicating that while the algorithm is universal, the implementation is not.
The order in which representations are learned is arbitrary and not consistent across runs.
The network's logits can be approximated as a sum of characters from a sparse set of representations.
Ablations confirm that the identified components are causally important for the task.
papers.limitation: The algorithm does not perfectly explain all logits due to limitations of the architecture (e.g., ReLU activations imperfectly implement matrix multiplication).
future_direction: Extending to other group theoretic tasks such as conjugacy, group actions, and automata.
Studying semigroups (which lack representation theory).
Investigating inductive biases of networks more broadly.
papers.abstract: Universality is a key hypothesis in mechanistic interpretability -- that different models learn similar features and circuits when trained on similar tasks. In this work, we study the universality hypothesis by examining how small neural networks learn to implement group composition. We present a novel algorithm by which neural networks may implement composition for any finite group via mathematical representation theory. We then show that networks consistently learn this algorithm by reverse engineering model logits and weights, and confirm our understanding using ablations. By studying networks of differing architectures trained on various groups, we find mixed evidence for universality: using our algorithm, we can completely characterize the family of circuits and features that networks learn on this task, but for a given network the precise circuits learned -- as well as the order they develop -- are arbitrary.

papers.title: Enhancing Chain-of-Thought Reasoning with Critical Representation Fine-tuning
papers.research_question: How can chain-of-thought reasoning in language models be enhanced by identifying and optimizing critical representations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Critical Representation Fine-Tuning (CRFT), a parameter-efficient method that identifies and optimizes critical representations in language models to enhance chain-of-thought reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: CRFT offers a lightweight and powerful alternative to traditional PEFT methods, highlighting the potential of representation-level optimization for chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
CRFT improves LLaMA-2-7B accuracy on GSM8K by 18.2% with only 0.016% parameters.
CRFT outperforms ReFT and other PEFT methods on various arithmetic and commonsense reasoning datasets.
CRFT is effective in few-shot learning, boosting one-shot accuracy by 16.4%.
Critical representations identified by CRFT have significant impact on output, as validated by noise perturbation experiments.
Interventions in earlier layers have greater impact on performance than later layers.
papers.abstract: Representation Fine-tuning (ReFT), a recently proposed Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) method, has attracted widespread attention for significantly improving parameter efficiency by editing representation space alone. In this work, we investigate applying ReFT to complex reasoning tasks. However, directly using the native ReFT method, which modifies fixed representations at the beginning and end of each layer, yields suboptimal performance, as these fixed-position representations have uncertain impact on the outputs. We observe that, in complex reasoning tasks, there often exist certain critical representations. These representations either integrate significant information from preceding layers or regulate subsequent layer representations. Through layer-by-layer propagation, they exert a substantial influence on the final output. Naturally, fine-tuning these critical representations has the potential to greatly enhance reasoning performance. Building upon these insights, we propose Critical Representation Fine-Tuning (CRFT), a novel method that identifies and optimizes these critical representations through information flow analysis. CRFT operates within a supervised learning framework, dynamically optimizing critical representations in a low-rank linear subspace while freezing the base model. The effectiveness and efficiency of our method are validated across eight benchmarks for arithmetic and commonsense reasoning, using LLaMA and Mistral model families. Furthermore, our method also adapts effectively to few-shot settings, boosting one-shot accuracy by 16.4%.
